articles.title: Lifecycle Lessons From CVE-2026-111460 in Industrial Networks
articles.excerpt: Lifecycle Lessons From CVE-2026-111460 in Industrial Networks CVE-2026-111460 is an end-of-life problem before it is a patch problem. The Moxa OnCell G3150A-LTE Series has a hard-coded HTTPS private k…
articles.body: Lifecycle Lessons From CVE-2026-111460 in Industrial Networks CVE-2026-111460 is an end-of-life problem before it is a patch problem. The Moxa OnCell G3150A-LTE Series has a hard-coded HTTPS private key and CA private key in firmware, every firmware version is affected, and the vendor offers a key-regeneration reset rather than fixed firmware. The case exposes a common gap between vulnerability response and the operational lifetime of remote industrial equipment. What happened Moxa describes CWE-321 use of a hard-coded cryptographic key. An unauthenticated remote attacker could obtain shared key material under certain conditions and impersonate affected devices that have not regenerated their keys. Management communications could lose confidentiality and integrity.

articles.title: Closed Testing With Test Accounts: License Testers, Test Payments, and What Testers Can and Cannot See
articles.excerpt: You have your 12 closed testers opted in. Now someone asks the question that stops a lot of first-time developers cold: "Should I test the payment flow with my own card?" Do not. Google Play has a bui…
articles.body: You have your 12 closed testers opted in. Now someone asks the question that stops a lot of first-time developers cold: "Should I test the payment flow with my own card?" Do not. Google Play has a built-in answer for exactly this — license testers and test payment methods — and using them is the difference between a clean test of your in-app purchases and a real charge, a real refund request, and a mess in your order history. A test account is not just a spare Gmail address. It is a Google account you control, added in the right places, that can install your closed-track build, make purchases that are never actually charged, and see exactly what a real tester sees — without touching real user data.

articles.title: Gemini API free tier 429: per-minute vs per-day limits, measured on four models
articles.excerpt: A Gemini API 429 on the free tier can mean two very different things: a per-minute limit that clears in seconds, or a per-day limit that clears at midnight Pacific. Most posts say "wait and retry" or…
articles.body: A Gemini API 429 on the free tier can mean two very different things: a per-minute limit that clears in seconds, or a per-day limit that clears at midnight Pacific. Most posts say "wait and retry" or "upgrade". That is true for one case and useless for the other. The error body already tells you which one it is. Read quotaId and retryDelay Per-minute: GenerateRequestsPerMinutePerProjectPerModel-FreeTier . Safe to retry after retryDelay . Per-day: GenerateRequestsPerDayPerProjectPerModel-FreeTier . Retrying is pointless until the reset. The limit is per project and per model, so a new key in the same project gives you nothing. The probe One tiny request, repeated until it fails. Each request asks for the single word ok with output capped at 20 tokens, so only the request count matters.

articles.title: Why is my piano late? Measuring audio latency on a normal Windows PC
articles.excerpt: I'm a CSE student at IIIT Raichur. In my first-year holidays I had a simple idea: I own a Casio CTK-2500, which has an aux output but no MIDI. Could I do live looping and play other instruments' sound…
articles.body: I'm a CSE student at IIIT Raichur. In my first-year holidays I had a simple idea: I own a Casio CTK-2500, which has an aux output but no MIDI. Could I do live looping and play other instruments' sounds using only my PC and software, with no audio interface? Day one: the sound arrives late I plugged the piano into the blue line-in jack and the speakers into the green jack. When I pressed a key, I heard it very late, around 150–200 ms by feel. I couldn't play a section in time. Looking it up, I learned that normal Windows audio is built for reliability, not for low delay. Trying faster drivers I installed WASAPI, ASIO4ALL and others. The delay dropped, but the sound had crackles and glitches.

articles.excerpt: AI agent takes unapproved actions even when laptop lid is closed and told not to.
articles.body: Researchers recently discovered unexpected behavior from Grok Bot, the AI agent platform from Elon Musk’s SpaceXSI. Over five days, Grok bots installed on two separate employee laptops made 31 requests to access data stored in employee calendar, email, Slack, and GitHub accounts. The bots performed the actions even though the employees had never ordered them and continued doing them even after employees instructed them to stop. The bots also denied having taken the actions at all. The behavior was reported Tuesday by NewCore, the maker of a managed gateway product that acts as an intermediary between AI agents and the tools and accounts they are assigned to work with.

articles.title: 'It looked like every star in the sky was falling': Eyewitnesses remember the great Leonid meteor storm of 1966
articles.excerpt: It was a spectacle many regard as the greatest meteor display on record.
articles.body: Overnight Nov. 17-18, 1966, the Leonid meteor storm thrilled stargazers during one extraordinary night when the stars themselves looked as though they were falling from the sky. At the peak of the shower, observers at Kitt Peak National Observatory in Arizona estimated an astonishing 40 meteors per second streaking across the sky. That's 2,400 shooting stars per minute, or a staggering 144,000 per hour. It was a spectacle that many regard as the greatest meteor display in recorded history. It's hard to imagine what it was like to experience such a spectacle. But who better to tell us than those who saw it with their own eyes? To mark the 60th anniversary of the great Leonid meteor storm of 1966, we asked those who saw it to share their memories.

articles.title: Satellites now outnumber the visible stars above most towns
articles.excerpt: More than 700 satellites are crossing the sky over an average mid-latitude town at any moment of the night, outnumbering in many cases the stars visible to the naked eye.
articles.body: More than 700 satellites are crossing the sky over an average mid-latitude town at any moment of the night, outnumbering in many cases the stars visible to the naked eye. That's based on an analysis of the trajectories of the 15,833 active satellites that currently circle the planet in low Earth orbit below an altitude of 1,200 miles (2,000 kilometers). Analyzing data from Oct. 12 and 18 this year, researchers found that with a completely unobstructed horizon, 710 satellites were crossing the sky in every single moment of the night above an average U.K. town. The results were published as a non-peer-reviewed study conducted by engineering firm Accu Components, and is based on satellite monitoring data from the U.S. Space Force available through the public website CelesTrak.

Original Annotated Milky Way versus Aurora Explanation: Are these two giant arches battling for control of the sky? No, but it sure looks like it! articles.title: California sues OpenAI over rogue AI hacking incidents
articles.excerpt: California is suing OpenAI after its AI agents broke out of their testing environment and hacked other companies, including Hugging Face. In a lawsuit filed Monday, Attorney General Rob Bonta accuses…
articles.body: California is suing OpenAI after its AI agents broke out of their testing environment and hacked other companies, including Hugging Face. In a lawsuit filed Monday , Attorney General Rob Bonta accuses OpenAI of violating consumer safety law by knowingly developing a "dangerous product without proper oversight," as reported earlier by Reuters . The lawsuit claims the cyberattack on Hugging Face "was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability." articles.body: Sam… thank you. | Image: Getty Images OpenAI CEO Sam Altman is once again addressing his controversial comments on PC RAM purchases. "I want to be clear, I want people to have a lot of RAM, I think everybody should be able to buy a lot of RAM for their own computer," Altman said today. "I think the home tinkering is great." The comments were made onstage at Semafor's Silicon Valley & The World summit on Monday. Altman's remarks on RAM stirred up controversy last month. In an appearance on the Cheeky Pint podcast , Altman said that it's "quite terrible" for everyone to have RAM in personal computers rather than in data centers.
